newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech opposition may seek rider on Germany pact.
newsitem.headline: Czech opposition may seek rider on Germany pact.

text.p: The main Czech opposition Social Democrats (CSSD) said on Monday they might want to add something to a Czech-German post-World War Two declaration that has been finalised and is awaiting signature.

The Czech Republic and Germany concluded nearly two years of delicate negotiations in December over the text of the joint declaration aimed at ending ill-feeling and suspicions lingering from World War Two and its aftermath.
The declaration expresses Bonn's sorrow for the 1938-45 Nazi occupation of the Czech lands and Prague's regret for Czech brutality in the post-war expulsion of ethnic Germans.
The text has been approved by both governments, which have each said it should not be changed by their parliaments.
It is expected to be signed by both countries' prime ministers and presidents in the coming weeks.

But Petr Sulak, a CSSD deputy and member of the foreign committee of the Czech parliament's lower house, which must ratify the agreement, told Reuters on Monday his party still had concerns about the text.
"The Social Democrats have views on certain formulations in the declaration which could in the future be a basis for negative tendencies from the German side," he said.
The CSSD has expressed conditional support for the text, but has been relunctant to announce its full backing.
Sulak declined to elaborate on what particular passages the party found troublesome, but said the problem did not include property issues.
The other two opposition parties in the Czech parliament, the ultra-right Republicans and the ex-Communists, have both categorically rejected the pact with Germany.
The government of Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus is two seats short of a majority in the lower house.
Diplomats have said German Chancellor Helmut Kohl is expected to visit Prague later this month to sign the document with Klaus, but a firm date has not been confirmed.
The parliaments of the two countries are then expected to discuss the text in February ahead of a formal ratifcation ceremony including both countries' presidents.
The chairman of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD). Oskar Lafontaine, said on a recent visit to Prague that his party would push for approval of the declaration.

Czech opponents of the text claim it fails to pay direct compensation to victims of Nazi agression, while German groups are furious that it avoids paying restitution for Prague's expropriation of property of so-called Sudeten Germans forced to leave the country.
